claim: Microscopic colitis is an inflammatory bowel disease divided into two subtypes: collagenous colitis and lymphocytic colitis.
source: Microscopic colitis is an inflammatory bowel disease divided into two subtypes: collagenous colitis and lymphocytic colitis.
evidence: This is a definitional statement presented in the abstract that establishes the classification of microscopic colitis.

claim: The incidence of microscopic colitis exceeds those of ulcerative and Crohn's disease among elderly people in some countries.
source: With an increasing incidence of microscopic colitis exceeding those of ulcerative and Crohn's disease among elderly people in some countries, microscopic colitis is a debilitating life experience.
evidence: This claim is supported by epidemiological data presented in the manuscript comparing incidence rates.

claim: The immune system and a dysregulated immune response play a key role in microscopic colitis combined with risk factors in genetically predisposed individuals.
source: The immune system and a dysregulated immune response seem to play a key role combined with risk factors (e.g. cigarette smoking) in genetically predisposed individuals.
evidence: This is a mechanistic claim about etiopathology based on scientific understanding presented in the manuscript.

claim: Microscopic colitis symptoms are characterized by recurrent or chronic nonbloody, watery diarrhea, urgency, weight loss, and a female preponderance.
source: The symptoms are characterized by recurrent or chronic nonbloody, watery diarrhea, urgency, weight loss, and a female preponderance.
evidence: This is a clinical description of symptoms based on observed patient presentations.

claim: Biomarkers are absent in microscopic colitis.
source: As biomarkers are absent, the diagnosis relies on colonoscopy with a histological assessment of biopsy specimens from all parts of the colon.
evidence: This is a statement about the current diagnostic limitations of microscopic colitis.

claim: The diagnosis of microscopic colitis relies on colonoscopy with histological assessment of biopsy specimens from all parts of the colon.
source: As biomarkers are absent, the diagnosis relies on colonoscopy with a histological assessment of biopsy specimens from all parts of the colon.
evidence: This is a statement about the diagnostic approach for microscopic colitis.

claim: Microscopic colitis is not associated with a risk of colorectal cancer.
source: Although the disease is not associated with a risk of colorectal cancer, a recent nationwide, population-based cohort study found an increased risk of lymphoma and lung cancer.
evidence: This claim is supported by epidemiological studies examining cancer risk in microscopic colitis patients.

claim: A recent nationwide, population-based cohort study found an increased risk of lymphoma and lung cancer in microscopic colitis patients.
source: Although the disease is not associated with a risk of colorectal cancer, a recent nationwide, population-based cohort study found an increased risk of lymphoma and lung cancer.
evidence: This claim is based on data from a specific cohort study mentioned in the manuscript.

claim: Budesonide is the first-line therapy for management of microscopic colitis.
source: Budesonide is the first-line therapy for management, whereas immunomodulatory drugs (including biologics) and drugs with antidiarrheal properties may be indicated in those failing, dependent, or intolerant to budesonide.
evidence: This is a treatment recommendation based on clinical trial data and guidelines.

claim: Immunomodulatory drugs (including biologics) and drugs with antidiarrheal properties may be indicated in patients failing, dependent, or intolerant to budesonide.
source: Budesonide is the first-line therapy for management, whereas immunomodulatory drugs (including biologics) and drugs with antidiarrheal properties may be indicated in those failing, dependent, or intolerant to budesonide.
evidence: This is a treatment recommendation for second-line therapy based on clinical experience.

claim: In microscopic colitis induced by checkpoint inhibitors, a more aggressive therapeutic approach with biologics introduced early seems reasonable.
source: In microscopic colitis induced by checkpoint inhibitors, a drug class used increasingly for a wide range of malignancies, a more aggressive therapeutic approach with biologics introduced early seems reasonable.
evidence: This is a treatment recommendation based on clinical observations of checkpoint inhibitor-induced microscopic colitis.

claim: Incomplete forms of microscopic colitis exist with the risk of being overlooked in routine clinical settings.
source: However, particular attention needs to be drawn to the existence of incomplete forms of microscopic colitis with the risk of being overlooked in routine clinical settings.
evidence: This is a clinical observation about diagnostic challenges in microscopic colitis.

claim: Microscopic colitis is a common cause of chronic or recurrent, nonbloody, watery diarrhea.
source: Microscopic colitis, of which two major histological subtypes (collagenous colitis and lymphocytic colitis) exist, is a common cause of chronic or recurrent, nonbloody, watery diarrhea.
evidence: This is a clinical characterization based on epidemiological and clinical data.

claim: The symptoms of microscopic colitis are nonspecific and the diagnosis requires histology.
source: Since the symptoms of microscopic colitis are nonspecific and the diagnosis requires histology, the disease risks being overlooked (Nielsen et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and describes diagnostic challenges.

claim: Microscopic colitis is affiliated to the umbrella diagnosis of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD).
source: It is affiliated to the umbrella diagnosis of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) (Escudero-Hernández et al., 2021)
evidence: This is a classification statement supported by a citation.

claim: Microscopic colitis is described by a clinicopathological triad characterized by a history of chronic or intermittent watery diarrhea, normal or almost normal endoscopic examination of the colon, and a distinct histological pattern.
source: and is described by a clinicopathological triad characterized by a history of chronic or intermittent watery diarrhea, normal or almost normal endoscopic examination of the colon (e.g., with slight edema, erythema, and/or loss of vascular pattern, although rarely more significant macroscopic changes are reported, including pseudomembranes and 'cat scratch changes') (Marlicz et al., 2004), as well as a distinct histological pattern when examined under a microscope – hence the name of this disorder.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about diagnostic criteria supported by citation.

claim: Microscopic colitis appears largely normal on endoscopic inspection and cross-sectional imaging.
source: In contrast, microscopic colitis appears largely normal on endoscopic inspection and cross-sectional imaging.
evidence: This is a clinical observation distinguishing microscopic colitis from classical IBD.

claim: Microscopic colitis is distinct from IBD histologically, with the former showing either a prominent intraepithelial lymphocytosis (lymphocytic colitis) or a thickened subepithelial collagen band (collagenous colitis).
source: In addition, microscopic colitis is distinct from IBD histologically, with the former showing either a prominent intraepithelial lymphocytosis (lymphocytic colitis) or a thickened subepithelial collagen band (collagenous colitis), while the latter (IBD) shows crypt abscesses, crypt architectural distortion (signifying chronic crypt destruction inflammation), and in some cases of Crohn's disease, granulomas (Vespa et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a histological comparison supported by citation.

claim: Ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease have their peak incidence in late adolescence and early adulthood.
source: Moreover, ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease have their peak incidence in late adolescence and early adulthood (Lophaven et al., 2004).
evidence: This is an epidemiological statement supported by citation.

claim: Most patients with microscopic colitis receive their diagnosis at an age of 60 or above.
source: Although most patients receive their diagnosis at an age of 60 or above, approximately 25% of patients get diagnosed before the age of 45 (Bonderup et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an epidemiological observation supported by citation.

claim: Approximately 25% of microscopic colitis patients get diagnosed before the age of 45.
source: Although most patients receive their diagnosis at an age of 60 or above, approximately 25% of patients get diagnosed before the age of 45 (Bonderup et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an epidemiological observation supported by citation.

claim: Microscopic colitis has been reported in children, which is very rare.
source: The disease has even been reported in children, which, however, is very rare (Windon et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a clinical observation supported by citation.

claim: A female preponderance exists in both collagenous and lymphocytic colitis, with a female-to-male ratio of 3.1 and 1.9, respectively.
source: A female preponderance exists in both collagenous and lymphocytic colitis, with a female-to-male ratio of 3.1 and 1.9, respectively (Tong et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an epidemiological observation supported by citation.

claim: A meta-analysis revealed a pooled worldwide incidence of microscopic colitis of 4.9 (95% CI 4.2–5.7) cases per 100,000 patient-years for collagenous colitis.
source: A meta-analysis has revealed a pooled worldwide incidence of microscopic colitis of 4.9 (95% CI 4.2–5.7) cases per 100,000 patient-years for collagenous colitis and 5.0 (95% CI 4.0–6.1) cases per 100,000 patient-years for lymphocytic colitis (Miehlke et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a quantitative epidemiological finding from a meta-analysis.

claim: A meta-analysis revealed a pooled worldwide incidence of microscopic colitis of 5.0 (95% CI 4.0–6.1) cases per 100,000 patient-years for lymphocytic colitis.
source: A meta-analysis has revealed a pooled worldwide incidence of microscopic colitis of 4.9 (95% CI 4.2–5.7) cases per 100,000 patient-years for collagenous colitis and 5.0 (95% CI 4.0–6.1) cases per 100,000 patient-years for lymphocytic colitis (Miehlke et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a quantitative epidemiological finding from a meta-analysis.

claim: Estimates of microscopic colitis incidence originate predominantly from North America and Europe.
source: Estimates of incidence originate predominantly from North America and Europe (Figure 1), and a substantial variation in incidence among regions has been observed.
evidence: This is an observation about the geographic distribution of epidemiological data, supported by Figure 1.

claim: A substantial variation in incidence of microscopic colitis among regions has been observed.
source: Estimates of incidence originate predominantly from North America and Europe (Figure 1), and a substantial variation in incidence among regions has been observed.
evidence: This is an epidemiological observation supported by data shown in Figure 1.

claim: In a recent Danish nationwide cohort study, the incidence of microscopic colitis (mean age at diagnosis: 65 years) was 24.3 per 100,000 patient-years in 2016.
source: For example, in a recent Danish nationwide cohort study, the incidence of microscopic colitis (mean age at the time of diagnosis: 65 years) was 24.3 per 100,000 patient-years in 2016 vs. 18.6 for ulcerative colitis and 9.1 for Crohn's disease per 100,000 patient-years in 2013 (Lophaven et al., 2004,; Weimers et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a specific epidemiological finding from a Danish cohort study.

claim: In Denmark in 2013, the incidence of ulcerative colitis was 18.6 per 100,000 patient-years and Crohn's disease was 9.1 per 100,000 patient-years.
source: For example, in a recent Danish nationwide cohort study, the incidence of microscopic colitis (mean age at the time of diagnosis: 65 years) was 24.3 per 100,000 patient-years in 2016 vs. 18.6 for ulcerative colitis and 9.1 for Crohn's disease per 100,000 patient-years in 2013 (Lophaven et al., 2004,; Weimers et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a specific epidemiological finding from a Danish cohort study.

claim: The incidence of microscopic colitis has increased over time.
source: In general, the incidence of microscopic colitis has increased over time (Tong et al., 2015)
evidence: This is a temporal epidemiological trend supported by citation.

claim: Improved recognition of microscopic colitis among gastroenterologists and pathologists may influence regional and temporal differences of the incidence.
source: Various factors, such as improved recognition of this disorder among gastroenterologists and pathologists, as well as varying presence of risk factors, may influence regional and temporal differences of the incidence.
evidence: This is an inference about factors affecting incidence trends.

claim: In a recent Danish nationwide cohort study, the incidence of microscopic colitis increased 10-fold, from 2.3 in 2001 to 24.3 cases per 100,000 patient-years in 2016.
source: Thus, in a recent Danish nationwide cohort study, the incidence of microscopic colitis was found to have increased 10-fold, from 2.3 in 2001 to 24.3 cases per 100,000 patient-years in 2016 (Weimers et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a specific epidemiological finding from a Danish cohort study.

claim: A regional Swiss study described a statistically significant increase in microscopic colitis incidence from 0.36 per 100,000 patient-years in 1994–1997 to 6.85 in 2017, with the mean age at diagnosis being 63 years.
source: Similarly, a regional Swiss study described a statistically significant increase in incidence from 0.36 per 100,000 patient-years in 1994–1997 to 6.85 in 2017, with the mean age at diagnosis being 63 years (Maye et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a specific epidemiological finding from a Swiss regional study.

claim: A similar trend of increasing incidence was observed in North America with subsequent stabilization in incidence.
source: A similar trend was observed in North America (Gentile et al., 2014) with subsequent stabilization in incidence (Tome et al., 2022b).
evidence: This is an epidemiological observation supported by citations.

claim: A number of factors are linked to an increased risk of microscopic colitis, including a positive association to a broad spectrum of autoimmune diseases.
source: A number of factors are linked to an increased risk of microscopic colitis, including a positive association to a broad spectrum of autoimmune diseases (Fedor et al., 2021), for example, celiac disease, type 1 diabetes mellitus, rheumatoid arthritis, polyarthritis, and thyroiditis (Wildt et al., 2021; Fernandez-Banares et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a risk factor association supported by citations.

claim: Bile acid malabsorption is associated with microscopic colitis.
source: Bile acid malabsorption is also associated ( Fernandez-Bañares et al., 2001).
evidence: This is an association supported by citation.

claim: Cigarette smoking is a risk factor associated with microscopic colitis.
source: Smoking status should be carefully reviewed as cigarette smoking is another risk factor associated with microscopic colitis (Jaruvongvanich et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a risk factor association supported by citation.

claim: The risk of microscopic colitis appears to be up to five times higher in current smokers, with the disease onset occurring a minimum 10 years earlier compared to nonsmokers.
source: The risk appears to be up to five times higher in current smokers, with the disease onset occurring a minimum 10 years earlier compared to nonsmokers (Jaruvongvanich et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a quantitative risk assessment supported by citation.

claim: A variety of environmental factors, including a wide range of drugs, have been associated with the pathophysiology of microscopic colitis.
source: A variety of environmental factors, including a wide range of drugs, have been associated with the pathophysiology of microscopic colitis; however, with variable evidence suggesting causality (Zylberberg et al., 2021; Morgan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a statement about environmental risk factors supported by citations.

claim: A certain cause–effect relationship between drug exposure and microscopic colitis has been described for proton pump inhibitors (PPIs), nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, or selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors.
source: Thus, a certain cause–effect relationship between drug exposure and microscopic colitis has been described for proton pump inhibitors (PPIs), nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, or selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (Verhaegh et al., 2016) both for current and recent use (Verhaegh et al., 2016; Bonderup et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a causal relationship claim supported by citations.

claim: When using diarrheal controls instead of healthy controls, the association with several medications lessens or resolves.
source: However, when using diarrheal controls instead of healthy controls, the association with several of these medications lessens or resolves (Zylberberg et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a methodological observation about study design effects supported by citation.

claim: A nationwide Swedish case–control study found that the prevalence of previous gastrointestinal (GI) infection was significantly higher in microscopic colitis than in controls.
source: Finally, a nationwide Swedish case–control study found that the prevalence of previous gastrointestinal (GI) infection was significantly higher in microscopic colitis than in controls (Khalili et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a finding from a case-control study supported by citation.

claim: A recent case–control study suggested that patients with microscopic colitis are less likely to be obese compared to those in diarrhea control groups.
source: Another recent case–control study suggested that patients with microscopic colitis are less likely to be obese compared to those in diarrhea control groups (Sandler et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a finding from a case-control study supported by citation.

claim: The pathogenesis of microscopic colitis is likely a result of dysbalanced immune response involving epithelial dysfunction, collagen metabolism, secretory diarrhea, and microbiota, combined with risk factors in genetically predisposed individuals.
source: The pathogenesis of microscopic colitis is still poorly elucidated, but it is likely a result of dysbalanced immune response involving epithelial dysfunction (Barmeyer et al., 2017), collagen metabolism, secretory diarrhea (Escudero-Hernández et al., 2020), and microbiota (Khalili et al., 2021; Aagaard et al., 2021; Figure 2), combined with the risk factors mentioned above in genetically predisposed individuals (Ianiro et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a mechanistic summary supported by multiple citations and Figure 2.

claim: A recent sequencing study showed microbiota from microscopic colitis to be significantly less diverse and compositionally distinct from healthy controls due to depletion of members of Clostridiales.
source: Thus, a recent sequencing study showed microbiota from microscopic colitis to be significantly less diverse and compositionally distinct from healthy controls due to depletion of members of Clostridiales; enriched for Prevotella and more likely dominated by this genus (Hertz et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a microbiome finding from a sequencing study supported by citation.

claim: Microbiota from microscopic colitis is enriched for Prevotella and more likely dominated by this genus.
source: Thus, a recent sequencing study showed microbiota from microscopic colitis to be significantly less diverse and compositionally distinct from healthy controls due to depletion of members of Clostridiales; enriched for Prevotella and more likely dominated by this genus (Hertz et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a microbiome finding from a sequencing study supported by citation.

claim: Two recent metagenomic studies revealed a lowered intestinal bacterial diversity and a reduction in the abundance of several genera in microscopic colitis, including Akkermansia and Ruminococcus.
source: Two recent metagenomic studies revealed a lowered intestinal bacterial diversity and a reduction in the abundance of several genera in microscopic colitis, including Akkermansia and Ruminococcus (Carstens et al., 2019; van Hemert et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a microbiome finding from metagenomic studies supported by citations.

claim: The de-enrichment of Akkermansia muciniphila was observed in a study using PCR.
source: The de-enrichment of Akkermansia muciniphila was additionally observed in a study using PCR (Fischer et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a microbiome finding from a PCR study supported by citation.

claim: A. muciniphila adheres to the intestinal epithelium and strengthens enterocyte monolayer integrity in vitro.
source: A. muciniphila adheres to the intestinal epithelium and strengthens enterocyte monolayer integrity in vitro, suggesting that a reduction may cause intestinal barrier dysfunction (Reunanen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a mechanistic finding from in vitro studies supported by citation.

claim: A reduction in A. muciniphila may cause intestinal barrier dysfunction.
source: A. muciniphila adheres to the intestinal epithelium and strengthens enterocyte monolayer integrity in vitro, suggesting that a reduction may cause intestinal barrier dysfunction (Reunanen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference based on in vitro findings supported by citation.

claim: A higher long-term risk of developing microscopic colitis was found in patients whose stool carried Campylobacter concisus.
source: More recently, a team of researchers found a higher long-term risk of developing microscopic colitis in patients whose stool carried Campylobacter concisus (Aagaard et al., 2021; Nielsen et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a risk association finding supported by citations.

claim: Campylobacter concisus is a commensal of the human oral microbiota, which occasionally may be isolated from stool samples.
source: Campylobacter concisus is a commensal of the human oral microbiota, which occasionally may be isolated from stool samples.
evidence: This is a microbiological fact about C. concisus.

claim: C. concisus is associated with epithelial sodium channel dysfunction and claudin-8-dependent barrier dysfunction.
source: C. concisus is associated with epithelial sodium channel dysfunction and claudin-8-dependent barrier dysfunction (Nattramilarasu et al., 2020), suggesting their involvement in the pathogenesis of microscopic colitis.
evidence: This is a mechanistic finding supported by citation.

claim: The intake of PPI and smoking influences bacterial flora.
source: Notably, the intake of PPI and smoking influences bacterial flora (Fujimori, 2015; Shanahan et al., 2018), especially the former may especially increase the abundance of oral microbes, such as C. concisus (Schlenker and Surawicz, 2009), suggesting that dysbiosis may be the mechanism by which these factors cause microscopic colitis.
evidence: This is a microbiome effect supported by citations.

claim: PPI intake may increase the abundance of oral microbes, such as C. concisus.
source: Notably, the intake of PPI and smoking influences bacterial flora (Fujimori, 2015; Shanahan et al., 2018), especially the former may especially increase the abundance of oral microbes, such as C. concisus (Schlenker and Surawicz, 2009), suggesting that dysbiosis may be the mechanism by which these factors cause microscopic colitis.
evidence: This is a microbiome effect supported by citation.

claim: Dysbiosis may be the mechanism by which PPI and smoking cause microscopic colitis.
source: Notably, the intake of PPI and smoking influences bacterial flora (Fujimori, 2015; Shanahan et al., 2018), especially the former may especially increase the abundance of oral microbes, such as C. concisus (Schlenker and Surawicz, 2009), suggesting that dysbiosis may be the mechanism by which these factors cause microscopic colitis.
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis based on microbiome data.

claim: Diarrhea itself might change the bacterial composition.
source: Meanwhile, diarrhea itself might also change the bacterial composition (Li et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an observation about the effect of diarrhea on microbiome supported by citation.

claim: It remains unclear whether the dysbiosis is causal or secondary to microscopic colitis.
source: Therefore, it remains unclear whether the dysbiosis is causal or secondary to microscopic colitis.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of uncertainty about causality.

claim: An altered intestinal microbiota composition is driven toward the composition of healthy controls once patients are in remission.
source: Nevertheless, an altered intestinal microbiota composition is driven toward the composition of healthy controls once patients are in remission (Rindom Krogsgaard et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a microbiome observation during remission supported by citation.

claim: A recent genetic immunochip study reported an association between the human leukocyte antigen (HLA) ancestral 8.1 haplotype and well-established collagenous colitis (314 patients) but not with lymphocytic colitis (122 patients).
source: A genetic component is of importance as well, and a recent genetic immunochip study with 4299 controls reported an association between the human leukocyte antigen (HLA) ancestral 8.1 haplotype and well-established collagenous colitis (314 patients) (Westerlind et al., 2017) but not with lymphocytic colitis (122 patients) (Westerlind et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a genetic association finding supported by citations.

claim: A significant genetic overlap was observed between ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease when comparing disease-associated single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs).
source: Furthermore, a significant genetic overlap was observed between ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease when comparing disease-associated single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) (Westerlind et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a genetic finding supported by citation.

claim: An array-based genetic association study on a cohort of 804 patients with collagenous colitis and more than 27,000 controls implicated independent risk and protective HLA loci in the risk of collagenous colitis.
source: An array-based genetic association study on a cohort of 804 patients with collagenous colitis and more than 27,000 controls aimed to investigate a common genetic basis between collagenous colitis and Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, or celiac disease (Stahl et al., 2020). In this detailed study, DNA was obtained from formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded samples of colonic biopsies collected in routine colonoscopies. Here, an independent risk and protective HLA loci were implicated in the risk of collagenous colitis (Stahl et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a genetic association finding from a GWAS supported by citation.

claim: The HLA-DQ haplotype has long been known to be predisposed toward celiac disease and to be associated with microscopic colitis.
source: In this context, the HLA-DQ haplotype has long been known to be predisposed toward celiac disease and to be associated with microscopic colitis (Fine et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a genetic association supported by citation.

claim: A cross-phenotype analysis identified a complex pattern of polygenic pleiotropy between collagenous colitis and other diseases, including celiac disease and IBD.
source: Moreover, a cross-phenotype analysis identified a complex pattern of polygenic pleiotropy between collagenous colitis and other diseases, including celiac disease and IBD (Stahl et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a genetic finding from cross-phenotype analysis supported by citation.

claim: A UK biobank study reported significant phenotypic associations with the use of PPIs, smoking status, and celiac disease in microscopic colitis.
source: This study stratified the data by drug use and employed GWAS to identify pharmacogenetic associations. Subsequently, a genetic risk score for IBD was calculated to quantify a genetic overlap with microscopic colitis (Green et al., 2019). Significant phenotypic associations with the use of PPIs (but with no other pharmacological risk factors), smoking status, and celiac disease were reported (Green et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a phenotypic association finding from a UK biobank study supported by citation.

claim: A UK biobank study confirmed the association with the major histocompatibility complex ancestral 8.1. haplotype.
source: This group confirmed the aforementioned, recently reported association with the major histocompatibility complex ancestral 8.1. haplotype (Westerlind et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a confirmation of a genetic association supported by citation.

claim: A UK biobank study reported suggestive evidence of a shared genetic risk between microscopic colitis and Crohn's disease, but not with ulcerative colitis.
source: By calculating risk scores, the researchers also reported suggestive evidence of a shared genetic risk with Crohn's disease, but not with ulcerative colitis (Green et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a genetic risk score finding supported by citation.

claim: The influence of SARS-CoV-2 infection on the GI system is well-established, with main symptoms being diarrhea, abdominal pain, loss of appetite, vomiting, nausea, and loss of taste.
source: The influence of SARS-CoV-2 infection on the GI system is well-established, with main symptoms being diarrhea, abdominal pain, loss of appetite, vomiting, nausea, and loss of taste (Jefremow and Neurath, 2021).
evidence: This is a clinical observation about SARS-CoV-2 GI effects supported by citation.

claim: Onset of lymphocytic colitis has been observed rarely following SARS-CoV-2 infection with consistently elevated levels of fecal calprotectin and persistent diarrhea.
source: However, onset of lymphocytic colitis has been observed rarely following SARS-CoV-2 infection with consistently elevated levels of fecal calprotectin and persistent diarrhea, even in the absence of fecal SARS-CoV-2 RNA (Nassar et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a clinical observation supported by citation.

claim: Lymphocytic colitis has been reported immediately after the second SARS-CoV-2 mRNA vaccine dose.
source: Moreover, lymphocytic colitis has been reported immediately after the second SARS-CoV-2 mRNA vaccine dose (Chey et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a clinical observation supported by citation.

claim: A review of the CDC's Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System revealed five mRNA vaccine-related cases of microscopic colitis following both Pfizer-BioNTech and Moderna inoculations.
source: The authors additionally performed a review of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention's Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System and revealed further five mRNA vaccine-related cases of microscopic colitis following both Pfizer-BioNTech and Moderna inoculations (three individuals developed severe diarrhea shortly after the second mRNA vaccine dose, whereas two individuals developed diarrhea approximately 1 month after receiving their second dose) (Chey et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a finding from a review of adverse event data supported by citation.

claim: No cases of microscopic colitis have been reported in patients receiving the Janssen single-dose vaccine.
source: No cases of microscopic colitis have, however, been reported in patients receiving the Janssen single-dose vaccine.
evidence: This is an observation about the absence of reported cases.

claim: Both lymphocytic colitis and collagenous colitis have been reported following therapy with immune checkpoint inhibitors.
source: With an increased use of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), that is neutralizing antibodies targeting the immune checkpoints T-lymphocyte-associated protein 4 (CTLA-4) or programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1)/programmed cell death ligand-1 (PD-L1) for various malignancies, both lymphocytic colitis and collagenous colitis have been reported following therapy with these drugs (Rampersad et al., 2021; Choi et al., 2019; Isidro et al., 2021; Pai et al., 2021; Zou et al., 2020)
evidence: This is a clinical observation supported by multiple citations.

claim: Checkpoint inhibitor-induced (autoimmune) enteritis and colitis are far more frequent intestinal complications than microscopic colitis.
source: although checkpoint inhibitor-induced (autoimmune) enteritis and colitis are far more frequent intestinal complications (Vaziri et al., 2022; Dougan et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a comparative frequency observation supported by citations.

claim: In case of diarrhea among patients presently on or previously treated with ICIs, the patients should always undergo a full colonoscopy.
source: Accordingly, in case of diarrhea among patients presently on or previously treated with ICIs, the patients should always undergo a full colonoscopy as immune-mediated colitis is a frequent adverse event.
evidence: This is a clinical recommendation based on the frequency of immune-mediated colitis.

claim: Even in the absence of any endoscopic abnormalities in ICI-treated patients, random biopsy samples should be obtained to assess the possibility of an underlying ICI-induced microscopic colitis.
source: Even in the absence of any endoscopic abnormalities, random biopsy samples should be obtained in order to assess the possibility of an underlying ICI-induced microscopic colitis (Dougan et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a clinical recommendation supported by citation.

claim: Budesonide may be successful for ICI-induced microscopic colitis.
source: Although budesonide may be successful for ICI-induced microscopic colitis, thus providing a compelling rationale for endoscopic identification (Hughes et al., 2019)
evidence: This is a treatment observation supported by citation.

claim: Microscopic colitis induced by ICIs may have a more aggravated, and even fatal, disease course.
source: it has been highlighted that microscopic colitis induced by ICIs may have a more aggravated, and even fatal, disease course (Fredrick et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a clinical observation about disease severity supported by citation.

claim: ICI-induced microscopic colitis may require more potent immunosuppressive therapeutic regimens with biologics at an early point and a greater need for hospitalization than non-ICI-induced microscopic colitis.
source: Such cases may require more potent immunosuppressive therapeutic regimens with biologics at an early point and a greater need for hospitalization than observed in a control group of non-ICI-induced microscopic colitis as well as traditional microscopic colitis without a history of cancer (Choi et al., 2019; Favara et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a treatment recommendation based on clinical observations supported by citations.

claim: In case of prescribing ICIs in patients with preexisting microscopic colitis, a close follow-up is recommended.
source: In case of prescribing ICIs in patients with preexisting microscopic colitis, a close follow-up is recommended (Fredrick et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a clinical recommendation supported by citation.

claim: One must always consider microscopic colitis in the event of unexplained intermittent symptoms of nonbloody, watery diarrhea.
source: One must always consider microscopic colitis in the event of unexplained intermittent symptoms of nonbloody, watery diarrhea.
evidence: This is a clinical recommendation based on symptom presentation.

claim: Patients with microscopic colitis often present additional symptoms, including urgency, fecal incontinence, abdominal discomfort, weight loss, arthralgias, and fatigue, impairing their quality of life.
source: Patients often present additional symptoms, including urgency, fecal incontinence, abdominal discomfort, weight loss, arthralgias, and fatigue, impairing their quality of life. (Pardi, 2017 ).
evidence: This is a clinical description of symptoms supported by citation.

claim: The onset of microscopic colitis is usually insidious, although sudden onset occurs in approximately 25% of patients.
source: The onset is usually insidious, although sudden onset occurs in approximately 25% of patients (Olesen et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a clinical observation about disease onset supported by citation.

claim: Many patients with microscopic colitis meet the diagnostic criteria for various other conditions like irritable bowel syndrome, functional diarrhea, celiac disease, bile acid diarrhea, lactose malabsorption, and small intestinal bacterial overgrowth.
source: As symptoms are typically nonspecific, many patients meet the diagnostic criteria for various other conditions like irritable bowel syndrome, functional diarrhea, celiac disease, bile acid diarrhea, lactose malabsorption, and small intestinal bacterial overgrowth. Accordingly, these diagnoses all have to be considered should a patient with microscopic colitis not respond to standard therapy (Nimri et al., 2021; Poon et al., 2021; Misselwitz et al., 2019; Shiha et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a clinical observation about diagnostic overlap supported by citations.

claim: The diagnosis of microscopic colitis is based on a full colonoscopy with histopathological assessment of multiple random biopsies obtained from the entire colon despite endoscopic absence of any macroscopic abnormalities.
source: The diagnosis of microscopic colitis is based on a full colonoscopy with histopathological assessment of multiple random biopsies obtained from the entire colon despite endoscopic absence of any macroscopic abnormalities.
evidence: This is a diagnostic standard based on clinical practice.

claim: A recent systematic review concluded that a minimum of six biopsies should be obtained in total (three from the ascending and three from the descending colon) to diagnose microscopic colitis.
source: In a recent systematic review aimed at determining the optimal sites and minimum number of colonic biopsies required to diagnose microscopic colitis from published studies, it was concluded that a minimum of six biopsies should be obtained in total (three from the ascending and three from the descending colon) (Malik et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a recommendation from a systematic review supported by citation.

claim: The histological findings of microscopic colitis are not uniform throughout the colon as the changes are more prominent in the proximal part of colon.
source: The histological findings of microscopic colitis are, however, not uniform throughout the colon as the changes are more prominent in the proximal part of colon.
evidence: This is a histological observation about disease distribution.

claim: It is recommended that biopsies from the rectum be avoided as the chance of missing the diagnosis is highest here.
source: Therefore, it is recommended that biopsies from the rectum be avoided as the chance of missing the diagnosis is highest here (Tanaka et al., 1992).
evidence: This is a diagnostic recommendation supported by citation.

claim: The minimal required histopathological criteria for the subtypes of microscopic colitis are achieved in >90% of the left-sided biopsies (rectum excluded), demonstrating a pancolitis in most patients.
source: The minimal required histopathological criteria for the subtypes of microscopic colitis seem to be achieved in >90% of the left-sided biopsies (rectum excluded), demonstrating a pancolitis in most patients with microscopic colitis (Fiehn et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a histological finding about disease distribution supported by citation.

claim: A flexible sigmoidoscopy is often inadequate and may miss the diagnosis in >20% of all patients if biopsies are not obtained above the rectosigmoid colon.
source: In this context, it has been revealed that a flexible sigmoidoscopy is often inadequate and may miss the diagnosis in >20% of all patients if biopsies are not obtained above the rectosigmoid colon (Chapman et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a diagnostic observation about the limitations of sigmoidoscopy supported by citation.

claim: The upper limit of the width of the normal collagen band in the subepithelial layer is approximately 5 µm.
source: When examining tissue specimens, the upper limit of the width of the normal collagen band in the subepithelial layer is approximately 5 µm.
evidence: This is a histological reference value.

claim: A collagen band >10 μM in width combined with an increased mixed inflammatory infiltrate in lamina propria defines collagenous colitis.
source: A collagen band >10 μM in width combined with an increased mixed inflammatory infiltrate in lamina propria defines collagenous colitis (Figure 3; Langner et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a histological diagnostic criterion supported by citation and Figure 3.

claim: The pathognomonic finding on biopsies in lymphocytic colitis is an intraepithelial lymphocytosis, defined as 20 or more intraepithelial lymphocytes (IEL) per 100 surface epithelial cells with a mixed infiltrate of acute and chronic inflammatory cells present in the lamina propria and a normal collagenous band (≤5 μM), typically without crypt distortion.
source: The pathognomonic finding on biopsies in lymphocytic colitis is an intraepithelial lymphocytosis, defined as 20 or more intraepithelial lymphocytes (IEL) per 100 surface epithelial cells with a mixed infiltrate of acute and chronic inflammatory cells present in the lamina propria and a normal collagenous band (≤5 μM), typically without crypt distortion (Figure 3; Langner et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a histological diagnostic criterion supported by citation and Figure 3.

claim: Mixed cases exist where histological changes of collagenous colitis are observed in some colonic segments, whereas other segments show changes of lymphocytic colitis.
source: However, mixed cases exist where histological changes of collagenous colitis are observed in some colonic segments, whereas other segments show changes of lymphocytic colitis (Fiehn et al., 2021; Engel et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a histological observation supported by citations.

claim: Some patients will change from one subtype of microscopic colitis to the other over time.
source: Moreover, some patients will change from one subtype to the other over time (Sonnenberg and Genta, 2022).
evidence: This is a clinical observation about disease evolution supported by citation.

claim: It is uncertain whether the two histological forms of microscopic colitis are really different entities or whether they could be different stages of a single pathological process.
source: Therefore, it is uncertain whether the two histological forms are really different entities or whether they could be different stages of a single pathological process, a phase of the process, or an individual response to different triggers.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of uncertainty about disease classification.

claim: A recent analysis confirmed a synchronous occurrence of microscopic colitis and IBD and transitions between the two diagnoses.
source: A recent analysis confirmed a synchronous occurrence of microscopic colitis and IBD and transitions between the two diagnoses (Sonnenberg and Genta, 2022).
evidence: This is a clinical observation supported by citation.

claim: A broader histological definition of microscopic colitis with less prominent abnormalities, termed 'incomplete microscopic colitis' or 'microscopic colitis not otherwise specified,' has been proposed.
source: Furthermore, in addition to the widely accepted histologic criteria (Table 1), a broader histological definition of microscopic colitis with less prominent abnormalities, termed 'incomplete microscopic colitis' or 'microscopic colitis not otherwise specified,' has been proposed (Langner et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a proposed diagnostic terminology supported by citation.

claim: In routine clinical practice, there is no difference in the treatment of lymphocytic colitis and collagenous colitis.
source: In routine clinical practice, there is no difference in the treatment of lymphocytic colitis and collagenous colitis, as demonstrated by the approach of current European and American guidelines (Miehlke et al., 2021; Pardi et al., 2016; Nguyen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a treatment approach supported by guidelines cited.

claim: No significant differences exist in treatment response with regard to commonly used medications between younger (i.e., ≤50 years) and older (i.e., >50 years) patients with microscopic colitis.
source: No significant differences exist in treatment response with regard to commonly used medications between younger (i.e., ≤50 years) and older (i.e., >50 years) patients with microscopic colitis (Sonnenberg and Genta, 2022 ; Kamboj et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a treatment response observation supported by citations.

claim: The primary treatment goal is to achieve a clinical remission of microscopic colitis.
source: The primary treatment goal is to achieve a clinical remission of microscopic colitis.
evidence: This is a treatment objective statement.

claim: In the frequent cases of a relapsing disease course, secondary goals are to maintain remission sufficiently and improve the patient's quality of life.
source: In the frequent cases of a relapsing disease course, secondary goals are to maintain remission sufficiently, and in this way to improve the patient's quality of life.
evidence: This is a treatment objective statement.

claim: It is unknown whether histological remission is an important goal in microscopic colitis.
source: It is unknown whether histological remission is an important goal, so in patients who respond clinically, repeat biopsies are not recommended.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of uncertainty about treatment goals.

claim: In patients who respond clinically to treatment, repeat biopsies are not recommended.
source: It is unknown whether histological remission is an important goal, so in patients who respond clinically, repeat biopsies are not recommended.
evidence: This is a clinical recommendation based on current knowledge.

claim: The first step in management is to consider elimination of exacerbating factors, including encouraging smoking cessation and withdrawing any culprit medications.
source: The first step in management is to consider elimination of exacerbating factors; that is, to encourage smoking cessation and withdraw any culprit medications, that is, drugs with a suspected chronological relationship between drug introduction and onset of diarrhea.
evidence: This is a management recommendation based on risk factor knowledge.

claim: Discontinuation of the offending drug leads to disease improvement in the majority of cases.
source: Although discontinuation of the offending drug leads to disease improvement in the majority of cases, (Hamdeh et al., 2021), there is no clear evidence yet of how it might predictably alter the disease course.
evidence: This is a clinical observation supported by citation.

claim: There is no clear evidence yet of how discontinuation of offending drugs might predictably alter the disease course of microscopic colitis.
source: Although discontinuation of the offending drug leads to disease improvement in the majority of cases, (Hamdeh et al., 2021), there is no clear evidence yet of how it might predictably alter the disease course.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of evidence limitations.

claim: Budesonide is the mainstay for induction and maintenance of remission in microscopic colitis, based on randomized placebo-controlled trials and meta-analyses.
source: Budesonide, a synthetic, locally acting glucocorticoid with topical effects in the GI tract, is the mainstay for induction and maintenance of remission in this disorder, based on randomized placebo-controlled trials and meta-analyses. (Chande et al., 2017; Kafil et al., 2017; Sebastian et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a treatment recommendation supported by multiple citations.

claim: Budesonide is recommended as first-line therapy according to both American Gastroenterological Association guidelines and the European Microscopic Colitis Group statements.
source: Budesonide is recommended as first-line therapy according to both American Gastroenterological Association guidelines and the European Microscopic Colitis Group statements (Miehlke et al., 2021; Pardi et al., 2016; Nguyen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a guideline recommendation supported by citations.

claim: Budesonide allows local selective therapy of the GI tract by high-affinity binding to the intracellular glucocorticoid receptor.
source: This second-generation glucocorticoid allows local selective therapy of the GI tract by high-affinity binding to the intracellular glucocorticoid receptor (Miehlke et al., 2018a).
evidence: This is a pharmacological mechanism supported by citation.

claim: Extensive (90%) first-pass metabolism within the liver and the mucosa of the small intestine reduce the systemic availability of budesonide.
source: Moreover, extensive (90%) first-pass metabolism within the liver and the mucosa of the small intestine reduce the systemic availability (Miehlke et al., 2018a), which diminishes the risk of side effects and obviates the need for dose tapering during induction therapy.
evidence: This is a pharmacokinetic property supported by citation.

claim: No cases of adrenal insufficiency have been reported in prospective clinical studies when discontinuing a daily dosage of 9 mg budesonide for 6–8 weeks without tapering.
source: Thus, no cases of adrenal insufficiency have been reported in prospective clinical studies when discontinuing a daily dosage of 9 mg for 6–8 weeks without tapering.
evidence: This is a safety observation from clinical studies.

claim: Budesonide administered orally has been assessed for induction of remission in four randomized-controlled trials of collagenous colitis and three of lymphocytic colitis.
source: Budesonide administered orally has been assessed for induction of remission in four randomized-controlled trials of collagenous colitis (Kafil et al., 2017) and three of lymphocytic colitis (Chande et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a summary of clinical trial evidence supported by citations.

claim: The proportions of patients in clinical remission after 6–8 weeks of budesonide treatment ranged from 72 to 91% of those with lymphocytic colitis, and from 73 to 100% of those with collagenous colitis.
source: The proportions of patients in clinical remission after 6–8 weeks of treatment ranged from 72 to 91% of those with lymphocytic colitis, and from 73 to 100% of those with collagenous colitis.
evidence: This is a quantitative efficacy finding from clinical trials.

claim: The frequency of watery diarrhea decreased quickly, usually within 2 weeks of budesonide treatment initiation.
source: The frequency of watery diarrhea decreased quickly, usually within 2 weeks of treatment initiation (Miehlke et al., 2018b).
evidence: This is a clinical response observation supported by citation.

claim: First-line treatment of active microscopic colitis is a dosage of 9 mg budesonide once daily for 8 weeks.
source: Accordingly, first-line treatment of active microscopic colitis is a dosage of 9 mg budesonide once daily for 8 weeks (Miehlke et al., 2018b).
evidence: This is a treatment recommendation supported by citation.

claim: Budesonide has shown efficacy in the management of incomplete microscopic colitis.
source: Budesonide has even shown efficacy in the management of incomplete microscopic colitis (Münch et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a treatment efficacy observation supported by citation.

claim: Recurrence is a frequent phenomenon after a short-term budesonide therapy.
source: As recurrence is a frequent phenomenon after a short-term budesonide therapy (Sebastian et al., 2019), maintenance therapy may be considered.
evidence: This is a clinical observation about disease course supported by citation.

claim: Randomized trials of maintenance therapy with 4.5 or 6 mg of budesonide per day for 6–12 months after remission revealed that remission was sustained in 60–75% of patients.
source: Randomized trials of maintenance therapy, in which 4.5 or 6 mg of budesonide was administered per day for 6–12 months after remission, revealed that remission was sustained in 60–75% of patients, and that treatment was well-tolerated without any specific safety issues (Bonderup et al., 2009; Miehlke et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a quantitative efficacy finding from randomized trials supported by citations.

claim: Budesonide maintenance therapy was well-tolerated without any specific safety issues.
source: Randomized trials of maintenance therapy, in which 4.5 or 6 mg of budesonide was administered per day for 6–12 months after remission, revealed that remission was sustained in 60–75% of patients, and that treatment was well-tolerated without any specific safety issues (Bonderup et al., 2009; Miehlke et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a safety observation from randomized trials supported by citations.

claim: Around 80% of patients were reported to have relapsed after withdrawal of long-term budesonide therapy.
source: Nevertheless, in one study, around 80% of patients were reported to have relapsed after withdrawal of long-term budesonide therapy (Münch et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a relapse rate finding supported by citation.

claim: In the event of relapse, the patient should be reassessed and retreated, aiming to taper to the lowest possible dose of budesonide.
source: In the event of relapse, the patient should accordingly be reassessed and retreated, aiming to taper to the lowest possible dose of budesonide, for example, 3 mg alternate days, but the duration of any maintenance therapy is yet unknown.
evidence: This is a treatment recommendation based on clinical practice.

claim: The duration of any budesonide maintenance therapy is yet unknown.
source: In the event of relapse, the patient should accordingly be reassessed and retreated, aiming to taper to the lowest possible dose of budesonide, for example, 3 mg alternate days, but the duration of any maintenance therapy is yet unknown.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of knowledge gap.

claim: Calcium and vitamin D supplementation should be recommended to the subgroup of patients requiring budesonide maintenance.
source: Moreover, as long-term use of glucocorticoids is controversial, calcium and vitamin D supplementation should be recommended to the subgroup of patients requiring budesonide maintenance.
evidence: This is a clinical recommendation to prevent side effects.

claim: Budesonide may have less impact on bone density than a traditional glucocorticoid like prednisolone.
source: Physicians often consider monitoring bone mineral density in patients treated with budesonide maintenance therapy, although budesonide may have less impact on bone density than a traditional glucocorticoid like prednisolone (Schoon et al., 2005)
evidence: This is a comparative safety observation supported by citation.

claim: A recent study reported a low risk of metabolic bone disease (and other steroid-related side effects) with budesonide that was not significantly different from patients not treated with budesonide.
source: and a recent study reported a low risk of metabolic bone disease (and other steroid-related side effects) that was not significantly different from patients not treated with budesonide (Tome et al., 2022a).
evidence: This is a safety finding from a recent study supported by citation.

claim: Loperamide has never been systematically studied in relation to microscopic colitis.
source: Even though there is not enough evidence to recommend loperamide, as this antidiarrheal medication has never been systematically studied in relation to microscopic colitis
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of evidence gap.

claim: Loperamide might be an option as symptomatic therapy in patients with urgency as well as mild microscopic colitis.
source: loperamide might, however, be an option as symptomatic therapy in patients with urgency as well as mild microscopic colitis.
evidence: This is a treatment suggestion based on clinical reasoning.

claim: In one large case series, antidiarrheal therapy by itself was able to induce remission in only a small fraction of patients with microscopic colitis.
source: However, in one large case series, antidiarrheal therapy by itself was able to induce remission in only a small fraction of patients (Pardi et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a clinical observation from a case series supported by citation.

claim: Cholestyramine may be helpful, especially in the substantial number of patients with microscopic colitis and coexisting bile acid malabsorption.
source: Cholestyramine (a bile acid-binding resin used for diarrhea due to bile acid malabsorption) may be helpful, especially in the substantial number of patients with microscopic colitis and coexisting bile acid malabsorption (Fernandez-Bañares et al., 2001; Ung et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a treatment recommendation supported by citations.

claim: Bile acid sequestrant therapy may be effective in decreasing budesonide dependence in half the patients with microscopic colitis.
source: Moreover, bile acid sequestrant therapy may be effective in decreasing budesonide dependence in half the patients with microscopic colitis (Northcutt et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a treatment efficacy observation supported by citation.

claim: A recent study suggested that a serum marker of bile acid malabsorption, 7-α-hydroxy-4-cholesten-3-one, may predict response to colesevelam in microscopic colitis.
source: A recent study suggested that a serum marker of bile acid malabsorption, 7-α-hydroxy-4-cholesten-3-one, may predict response to colesevelam in microscopic colitis (Saha et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a predictive biomarker finding supported by citation.

claim: Colesevelam is a bile acid sequestrant shown to be efficacious in bile acid malabsorption in Crohn's disease.
source: Colesevelam is a bile acid sequestrant shown to be efficacious in bile acid malabsorption in Crohn's disease (Beigel et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a treatment efficacy observation in Crohn's disease supported by citation.

claim: Bismuth subsalicylate has antisecretory and anti-inflammatory properties and reduces diarrhea in microscopic colitis.
source: Bismuth subsalicylate, having antisecretory and anti-inflammatory properties, reduces diarrhea in microscopic colitis.
evidence: This is a pharmacological property and clinical effect statement.

claim: The antidiarrheal mechanism of action of bismuth subsalicylate still has to be determined.
source: However, the antidiarrheal mechanism of action still has to be determined (Ericsson et al., 1990).
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of knowledge gap supported by citation.

claim: Bismuth subsalicylate (nine tablets [262 mg each] per day in three divided doses) performed better than placebo in a randomized trial.
source: Bismuth subsalicylate (nine tablets [262 mg each] per day in three divided doses) performed better than placebo in a randomized trial (Fine et al., 1999).
evidence: This is a treatment efficacy finding from a randomized trial supported by citation.

claim: In a study of 94 patients treated with bismuth subsalicylate, 57% patients showed complete response, 21% had partial response, and 21% had no response.
source: In another study, the clinical response and recurrence rates in 94 patients (median age of 69 years; 91% females, 52% with lymphocytic colitis) treated with this drug were assessed (Tariq et al., 2017). The daily dose of bismuth subsalicylate was six tablets in 12 patients, eight tablets in 20 patients, and nine tablets in 62 patients. Overall, 57% patients showed complete response, 21% had partial response, and 21% had no response.
evidence: This is a quantitative efficacy finding from a clinical study supported by citation.

claim: Long-term use of bismuth subsalicylate is associated with the risk of neurotoxicity.
source: In this context, it is noteworthy that long-term use of this drug is associated with the risk of neurotoxicity (Borbinha et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a safety concern supported by citation.

claim: Thiopurines are not indicated as induction therapy for microscopic colitis because the onset of action is delayed (10–12 weeks).
source: When symptoms are truly refractory and considerably impact the quality of life, immunomodulating therapy with thiopurines (i.e., azathioprine [2–2.5 mg/kg per day] or mercaptopurine [1–1.5 mg/kg per day]) for maintenance of clinical remission may be initiated, but as the onset of action is delayed (10–12 weeks), thiopurines are not indicated as induction therapy (Nielsen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a treatment recommendation based on pharmacological properties supported by citation.

claim: In a cohort study of budesonide-refractory, -dependent, or -intolerant patients, complete or partial responses to thiopurines were observed in 43% of patients with collagenous colitis and 22% with lymphocytic colitis.
source: In a cohort study of budesonide-refractory, -dependent, or -intolerant patients (Cotter et al., 2017), thiopurines were used in 49 patients for a median duration of 4 months (IQR 1.5–15.0). Complete or partial responses were observed in 43% of patients with collagenous colitis and 22% with lymphocytic colitis.
evidence: This is a quantitative efficacy finding from a cohort study supported by citation.

claim: In a multicenter retrospective case series, 13 (28%) of 46 patients treated with azathioprine achieved and maintained clinical remission for up to 57 months, whereas 31 (67%) patients developed intolerance causing treatment cessation.
source: In a multicenter and retrospective case series, 13 (28%) of 46 patients treated with azathioprine achieved and maintained clinical remission for up to 57 months, whereas 31 (67%) patients developed intolerance causing treatment cessation (Münch et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a quantitative efficacy and safety finding from a case series supported by citation.

claim: Among 13 patients switched from azathioprine to mercaptopurine, six (46%) regained clinical remission.
source: Thirteen of these patients were subsequently switched to mercaptopurine, among whom six (46%) regained clinical remission.
evidence: This is a quantitative efficacy finding from a case series.

claim: Overall, 19 (41%) patients responded to thiopurine treatment in a multicenter case series.
source: Thus, overall, 19 (41%) patients responded to the treatment.
evidence: This is a quantitative efficacy summary from a case series.

claim: It is recommended that thiopurines should be administered for a minimum of 1 year, and perhaps even longer, in case of a beneficial response.
source: Although it is still not clear as to how long thiopurines should be administered in case of a beneficial response, it is recommended that they should be administered for a minimum of 1 year, and perhaps even longer.
evidence: This is a treatment duration recommendation based on clinical practice.

claim: A meta-analysis of 11 articles including 75 patients with severe microscopic colitis showed a response rate of 77% at 3–6 weeks and 67% at 12–16 weeks to biologicals.
source: A meta-analysis of 11 articles (four with infliximab and adalimumab, two with adalimumab, and five with vedolizumab), including 75 patients with severe microscopic colitis, showed a response rate of 77% at 3–6 weeks and 67% at 12–16 weeks, and 55% were able to achieve remission at 12–16 weeks (Taneja et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a quantitative efficacy finding from a meta-analysis supported by citation.

claim: In a meta-analysis of biologicals for microscopic colitis, 55% of patients were able to achieve remission at 12–16 weeks.
source: A meta-analysis of 11 articles (four with infliximab and adalimumab, two with adalimumab, and five with vedolizumab), including 75 patients with severe microscopic colitis, showed a response rate of 77% at 3–6 weeks and 67% at 12–16 weeks, and 55% were able to achieve remission at 12–16 weeks (Taneja et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a quantitative efficacy finding from a meta-analysis supported by citation.

claim: A recent multicenter cohort study showed that about half of the patients treated with TNF inhibitors for microscopic colitis achieved clinical remission following budesonide failure.
source: Moreover, a recent multicenter cohort study was the first to show that about half of the patients treated with TNF inhibitors for microscopic colitis achieved clinical remission following budesonide failure (Boivineau et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a quantitative efficacy finding from a cohort study supported by citation.

claim: Current research suggests that prednisolone is less effective than budesonide for both collagenous and lymphocytic colitis.
source: However, current research, including only one placebo-controlled trial with prednisolone (Munck et al., 2003), a population-based cohort study, (Gentile et al., 2013), and a meta-analysis (Stewart et al., 2011), suggests that prednisolone is less effective than budesonide for both collagenous and lymphocytic colitis.
evidence: This is a comparative efficacy finding supported by multiple citations.

claim: Prednisolone is not recommended for use in microscopic colitis.
source: Accordingly, this drug is not recommended for use in microscopic colitis (Miehlke et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a treatment recommendation supported by guideline citation.

claim: One study has indicated an effect of methotrexate in microscopic colitis, but 75% of the patients received concomitant budesonide.
source: One study has indicated an effect of methotrexate in microscopic colitis (Cotter et al., 2017). However, 75% of the patients in the study received concomitant budesonide, which limits the conclusions to be drawn about methotrexate as monotherapy.
evidence: This is a treatment efficacy observation with methodological limitations supported by citation.

claim: Other studies have described a relative ineffectiveness of methotrexate in microscopic colitis.
source: Meanwhile, other studies have described a relative ineffectiveness of methotrexate in microscopic colitis (Münch et al., 2013; Münch et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a treatment efficacy observation supported by citations.

claim: Methotrexate is not recommended for microscopic colitis management.
source: Therefore, this drug is not recommended for microscopic colitis management.
evidence: This is a treatment recommendation based on efficacy data.

claim: Mesalazine administered in a dose of 3 g per day for 8 weeks was not superior to placebo in patients with collagenous colitis or lymphocytic colitis.
source: Mesalazine administered in a dose of 3 g per day for 8 weeks was not superior to placebo in patients with collagenous colitis (Miehlke et al., 2014) or lymphocytic colitis (Miehlke et al., 2018b).
evidence: This is a treatment efficacy finding from clinical trials supported by citations.

claim: 5-aminosalicylic acid is not recommended as a therapeutic option for microscopic colitis.
source: Based on these data and supported by real-life experience for induction of remission in both collagenous and lymphocytic colitis (no studies for the maintenance of remission are available) (Bohr et al., 1996), 5-aminosalicylic acid is not recommended as a therapeutic option.
evidence: This is a treatment recommendation based on clinical trial data supported by citations.

claim: Data on the role of surgery in microscopic colitis are limited to isolated case reports.
source: Data on the role of surgery (i.e., subtotal colectomy, diverting ileostomy, or an ileal pouch-anal anastomosis) are limited to isolated case reports and should be regarded as the ultimate treatment option to be reserved for patients with a disease course refractory to all other medical therapies or when effective medication cannot be tolerated (Bislenghi et al., 2022 ; Münch et al., 2005; Järnerot et al., 1996).
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of limited evidence supported by citations.

claim: Surgery should be regarded as the ultimate treatment option to be reserved for patients with microscopic colitis refractory to all other medical therapies or when effective medication cannot be tolerated.
source: Data on the role of surgery (i.e., subtotal colectomy, diverting ileostomy, or an ileal pouch-anal anastomosis) are limited to isolated case reports and should be regarded as the ultimate treatment option to be reserved for patients with a disease course refractory to all other medical therapies or when effective medication cannot be tolerated (Bislenghi et al., 2022 ; Münch et al., 2005; Järnerot et al., 1996).
evidence: This is a treatment recommendation based on clinical practice supported by citations.

claim: Several studies have demonstrated an association between Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis and the risk of colorectal cancer.
source: Although several studies have demonstrated an association between Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis and the risk of colorectal cancer (Beaugerie and Itzkowitz, 2015; Olén et al., 2020b; Olén et al., 2020a)
evidence: This is an established association in IBD supported by citations.

claim: Previous studies focusing on the risk of colorectal cancer in microscopic colitis have not revealed an association.
source: previous studies focusing on the risk of colorectal cancer in microscopic colitis have not revealed such an association (Loreau et al., 2019; Levy et al., 2019; Borsotti et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a finding about the absence of association supported by citations.

claim: A systemic review and meta-analysis of 12 studies comprising 50,795 patients with microscopic colitis found a lower risk of colonic adenomas and colorectal cancer.
source: A systemic review and meta-analysis of 12 studies comprising 50,795 patients with microscopic colitis even found a lower risk of colonic adenomas and colorectal cancer (Liu et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a finding from a systematic review and meta-analysis supported by citation.

claim: A Swedish nationwide, population-based cohort study revealed an 8% elevated risk of overall cancer in individuals with microscopic colitis compared with reference individuals.
source: Nevertheless, a Swedish nationwide, population-based cohort study recently examined the association between microscopic colitis and overall risk of cancer as well as of some important cancer subtypes (Bergman et al., 2020). In this first large-scale study, an 8% elevated risk of overall cancer was revealed in individuals with microscopic colitis compared with reference individuals. (Bergman et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a quantitative risk finding from a cohort study supported by citation.

claim: A Swedish cohort study discovered an increased risk of lymphoma and lung cancer in patients with microscopic colitis.
source: Specifically, an increased risk of lymphoma and lung cancer was discovered in patients with microscopic colitis, even when performing a sensitivity analysis to account for the influence of immunomodulatory drugs on the risk for lymphoma, although a confounder for lung cancer may probably be due to a higher prevalence of smoking among patients with microscopic colitis (Bergman et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a specific cancer risk finding from a cohort study supported by citation.

claim: There were no associations found between microscopic colitis and breast, bladder, or colorectal cancers or with other GI malignancies.
source: However, there were no associations found with breast, bladder, or colorectal cancers or with other GI malignancies (Bergman et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a finding about the absence of associations supported by citation.

claim: The risk of cancer in microscopic colitis did not increase with the duration of disease.
source: Moreover, the study demonstrated that the risk of cancer did not increase with the duration of disease (Bergman et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a temporal risk finding from a cohort study supported by citation.

claim: Repeated colonoscopy with biopsies is seemingly not required in microscopic colitis, unless a patient's progress mandates further evaluation or suggests a possible alternative diagnosis.
source: Consequently, repeated colonoscopy with biopsies is seemingly not required in microscopic colitis, unless a patient's progress mandates further evaluation or suggests a possible alternative diagnosis.
evidence: This is a clinical recommendation based on cancer risk data.

claim: In a cohort of 318 patients with microscopic colitis with complete 1-year follow-up, 49% had a chronic active or relapsing disease course; 40% achieved sustained remission after treatment, and 11% had a quiescent course.
source: In a recent study, the clinical course over time in a cohort of 318 patients with microscopic colitis and a mean age of 64 years with complete 1-year follow-up revealed that 49% had a chronic active or relapsing disease course; 40% achieved sustained remission after treatment, and 11% had a quiescent course (Verhaegh et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding about disease course from a cohort study supported by citation.

claim: In general, symptoms and quality of life improved after 3 months of follow-up in microscopic colitis patients.
source: In general, symptoms and quality of life improved after 3 months of follow-up.
evidence: This is a clinical outcome observation.

claim: A relapsing or chronic active disease course was associated with considerably more symptoms and an impaired quality of life after 1 year.
source: A relapsing or chronic active disease course was associated with considerably more symptoms and an impaired quality of life after 1 year (Verhaegh et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a quality of life finding supported by citation.

claim: A study evaluating the natural history of microscopic colitis with a median follow-up of 8 years revealed that 75% of patients achieved prolonged remission without therapy for more than a year.
source: Previously, another study evaluating the natural history of microscopic colitis with a median follow-up of 8 years revealed that 75% of patients achieved prolonged remission without therapy for more than a year (Fernández-Bañares et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a natural history finding from a long-term study supported by citation.

claim: 93% of patients achieving remission spontaneously went on to have prolonged remission, whereas only 61% of those who achieved drug-induced remission had prolonged remission for more than a year.
source: Remarkably, 93% of patients achieving remission spontaneously went on to have prolonged remission, whereas only 61% of those who achieved drug-induced remission had prolonged remission for more than a year (Fernández-Bañares et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a comparative outcome finding supported by citation.

claim: Patients with microscopic colitis should be offered a regular follow-up until the symptoms resolve, and at least every 12 months thereafter.
source: Patients should be offered a regular follow-up until the symptoms resolve, and at least every 12 months thereafter with the goal of maintaining control over the chronic disorder and ensuring easy access to treatment at a specialized outpatient clinic in case of flaring up of the disease.

claim: In case patients require long-standing glucocorticoid treatment to control their disease, supplementation of calcium and vitamin D is recommended, and these individuals should be monitored regarding osteoporosis.
